content:
I was fortunate to join Bill Binch at 3 Battery CRO dinners over the past 4 weeks.

Consensus is that the promise of AI is there, but its not showing up in per AE productivity yet.

A few takeaways from these conversations with 35 GTM leaders:

(1) The best reps are getting even stronger with AI. For savvy reps, AI is shortening ramp time, prep time, and maximizing buyer facing time. Intellectually curious reps are winning. For weaker reps, AI can reinforce bad habits (poor listening skills, less critical thinking on deals).

(2) Reps building with AI is a tricky topic. Leader don’t want to stifle creativity, but need guardrails on quality, output, and time invested. General consensus was sales reps need to focus on selling, while RevOps/GTM engineers build apps. A consistent horror story was a rep spending 50+ hours and $5k on tokens to build a product that could be bought for $100/mo.

(3) Transactional vs an enterprise sales are diverging even more. Transactional teams are automating as much as possible, including customer touch points. The life of the enterprise seller hasn’t changed much. Going in person, building raport and real customer relationships are as important as they’ve ever been.

2027 is going to be a big year for AI in go-to-market.

The metric revenue leaders are all tracking is per AE productivity to ensure AI is driving positive, measurable impact.

content:
There are only 37 selling days left in 2026. If you're an AE behind on quota, here's exactly how I'd approach the rest of Q4:

I'd start by working backwards from the holiday calendar.

Thanksgiving is November 26, and momentum tends to slow down considerably around then. December has more selling days than last year, but realistically, you have until December 23 before buyers start checking out.
That leaves you with a much shorter selling window than you might think to get to quota. 

Here's what I'd prioritize:

(1) Self-source 1 new opportunity every week until Thanksgiving

If you're behind on quota, you can't afford to sit around waiting for inbound. Make 90 minutes a day to find these easy wins.

(2) Review your closed-lost opportunities from Q1 and Q2

Look for deals where there was interest and fit, but the timing wasn't right. A lot can change in 6 months. I'd reach back out now and see if there's an opportunity to restart those conversations.

(3) Revisit your existing network

Go through the people you've reached out to this year who showed some interest but never converted into an opportunity. And spot customers you sold to or got close to closing that may have switched companies.

(4) Get ahead of any complicated sales processes

If you're running trials, data or workflow validations, or deals that require a lot of back-and-forth, get those on the calendar now. Plan ahead with the holidays. Ideally, you're wrapping this work up before Thanksgiving or have a clear plan for picking things back up immediately after Thanksgiving.

There's still time to make up ground before the end of the year. But I'd treat the next few weeks as some of the most important selling days you have left on the calendar.

We analyzed 25M+ outbound emails across hundreds of Unify customers to identify what's getting replies in 2026. A lot of old ‘best practices’ are dying.

The teams posting 2-3x industry average reply rates are getting a handful of details right that most teams overlook. 

Here's some of what our data shows:

(1) Emails with an emoji in the subject line get 38% more replies. Only 5% of outbound emails use them - one of the biggest levers in the dataset.

(2) Emails with dollar signs or ROI claims see a 15% drop in reply rates. Before trust is established, money talk reads as a pitch.

(3) P.S. lines correlate with a 10% reply drop, but nearly half of all emails still include one. If it's worth saying, put it in the body.

(4) Signal-driven openers get 2x the reply rate of any other opener style, but only 3.8% of outbound emails use them. It's the single biggest whitespace in outbound right now.

(5) AI-personalized emails get 57% more replies, but not all personalization is equal. Deep research delivers 4x the baseline, while title-only drops 26% below it.

We pulled all our findings into a 19-page report that includes winning subject line patterns, copy frameworks, and best-practice email examples you can steal.

In the last 5 years, the median time to promotion from SDR to AE was 12 months. 

The fastest industries do it in as little as 8.

This is data from our study of 180,000+ SDRs & BDRs for our Path to AE report. Across the industries we charted, the gap between the fastest and slowest median is about 3 months, but the gap between a fast SDR and a slow SDR in the same industry is 10-12 months. 

Real Estate (small companies): the middle half of SDRs got promoted somewhere between 5 and 16 months.

Logistics (large companies): 8 to 20 months.

Hospitals and Health Care (large companies): 8 to 20 months.

Industry isn't the variable that decides your timeline - company size matters more than industry does. In the same industry, larger companies typically took 1-3 months longer to make the promotion.

What I'd take from this if I were a SDR/BDR right now:

Don't switch industries to get promoted faster. The data doesn't support it.

Do learn your industry's unique path. If most AEs in your space get there by switching companies, plan for that.

And ask your company how many of their AEs came from internal promotions.

I'm incredibly bullish on the future of SDRs. But I also think there are going to be a lot fewer of them in the next few years.

Last Tuesday, we hosted a debate at the Unify office during SF Tech Week on whether AI will replace SDRs, and I loved digging into this with Benjamin Douablin, Brian Weinberger, and Sunny Chauhan.

My take is that the SDR role is going to change pretty dramatically.

One thing I'm absolutely convinced of is that the phones aren't going anywhere.

Outbound is still insanely important. If you're not generating at 50% of your business through outbound, you're leaving demand on the table that your competitors are going after.

There's another reason I'm so bullish on SDRs: they're one of the best talent pipelines a sales organization can have.

Some of your best future AEs and CSMs are going to come from your SDR team. There's so much value in having people learn how to prospect and develop that foundation before moving into other roles.

So yes, I think AI will change what the SDR role looks like. But I don't see it disappearing anytime soon.

Huge thanks to Benjamin, Brian, and Sunny for a great conversation, and to everyone who came out.

(3) Our sales team became a bottleneck between users and the product

Our whole job as product builders is to make it as easy as possible for people to try what we build.

So we ripped the Band-Aid off and went self-serve.

The early results have been strong:

→ We have X00 paid self-serve customers
→ Sales trials are 10x easier to run
→ We have 5-7% free-to-paid conversion with very little optimization

There were real risks to moving from sales-led to PLG, especially around cannibalization. In our case it was 100% the right move.

content:
In April, Ethan and Neema sold me on folding our automated outbound and SDR programs together.

In May the team landed at 131% to quota.

The reason it worked is simpler than you'd think. We used to run them separately - automated outbound on one track, the SDR team on another.

But when the 2 programs run separately, you have 2 cold funnels. Outbound automation was converting leads to warm, but nobody was there to close and book the meeting. The NBRs were working cold on their own track.

Fold them together and the dynamic changes. Automated outbound warms the lead, and an SDR picks it up at exactly the right moment.

Now when a rep sees that a prospect just hit our website, they can just pick up the phone and call them. It's insanely natural.

Unify makes it easy for sellers to focus on the highest-value things in a given day. The 2 programs working together - instead of side by side - is what makes that possible. Our SDR team has been putting up some of the strongest numbers we've seen as a result.

Shoutout to Ethan and Neema for pushing for it and to the NBR team for proving them right.

content:
For years, top 1% outbound systems depended on a RevOps or GTM engineer who knew how every workflow worked. That's finally starting to change.

The old model was basically:

→ Hire one highly technical person
→ Have them build all of your workflows, automations, routing, research, etc
→ Leave the rest of the team to depend on them to keep it all running

The obvious risk with the old model is that GTM teams have a lot of turnover. When that person leaves, a huge amount of context leaves with them.

AI is starting to flip this model. Now, individual sellers can create and run their own workflows in natural language. GTM engineering used to have to manually configure email and phone waterfalls. Now sellers can prompt straight to the perfect waterfall for their specific industry.

Our own Unify reps are already using our revenue harness to automate work with virtually no technical knowledge of the underlying system.

I think that’s where a lot of GTM software is headed over the next few years: giving reps access to the leverage that used to sit with one GTM engineer.

For example, if you're applying for a BDR role at a startup you should prove you can do the job you're applying for by treating that potential job just like you would your sales process.

content:
In 2026, cold outbound email is hard to get right. 

But we still get hundreds of responses a month at Unify through warm outbound.

These are the 9 copywriting rules we always follow:

1. Don't sound like marketing. Most outbound dies because it sounds overproduced, generic, feature-heavy, or "thought leadership"-y. The fix is shorter sentences, conversational phrasing, concrete language, no buzzwords unless they're buyer-native. "Trigger outreach when accounts actually show intent" beats "revolutionize your GTM motion."

2. Lead with their world, not yours. Strong outbound starts with a pattern, observation, timing event, operational pain, or change in behavior. Not "Unify is a platform that..." The prospect should feel "this person understands what's happening in my org" before "this person wants something from me."

3. Curiosity beats persuasion. The goal of cold isn't to convince, educate fully, or close. It's to create "interesting, tell me more." Good CTAs sound like "worth comparing notes?", "is that something you're exploring?", "want me to send a few ideas?" Not "book 30 mins."

4. Specificity creates credibility. Never "ton of value," "powerful," "best-in-class," "drive efficiency." Instead: mention the signal, the workflow, the timing, the operational change.

5. Timing matters more than personalization. Most "personalization" is fake ("saw your recent post," "love what you're building"). Real relevance is: why now? what changed? what signal exists? why should they care today? This is exactly where Unify's signal layer wins.

6. Good outbound creates recognition. The best cold emails make someone think "yeah, that's actually true." Not "wow this company sounds impressive." Recognition beats persuasion.

7. One idea per message. One problem, one observation, one signal, one CTA. Most reps overload.

8. Social proof supports, not dominates. "Teams Perplexity" works. A giant customer flex paragraph doesn't. Proof reduces risk and adds legitimacy; it isn't the message.

9. The CTA should feel easy to answer. Yes/no questions work. Calendar requests don't, until interest exists.

Shoutout to Ethan Dursht for the killer copy tips

content:
Over the past 3 years, Unify's growth team generated 10,420 meetings with just 3-4 people.
 
For context, the industry benchmark is 15 meetings per SDR/month.
 
It's not perfectly apples-to-apples, but a 4-person team over 3 years at that pace would produce 2,160 meetings.
 
We did 4.8x that. For 3 years, we've been operating like a 19-person team.
 
Here's how we built the system:
 
In the early days it was all hustle. We hadn't set up paid or automated outbound. I started founder-led content and we pushed referrals and investor intros. We were grinding and it was working, but we knew it wouldn't scale.
 
Our first inflection point came in mid 2024.
 
November 2024 is when I first crossed 10k followers and my follower growth started accelerating.
 
During this time, we turned on paid acquisition and automated outbound. That's when things clicked and meetings nearly tripled.
 
By investing early in founder-led content and automated outbound, we built two flywheels:
 
1/ Founder-led content → inbound engine
 
39% of all meetings came from inbound and much of it was driven by consistent founder-led LinkedIn content that built trust over time. With the foundation in place, incremental effort now compounds and scales our top of funnel.
 
2/ Automated outbound → reaching thousands of accounts with 1-2 people
 
We drove 2,098 meetings from automated outbound.
 
With just 1-2 people running it at any one point in time, we were able to get coverage across thousands of accounts across our TAM.
 
If you're not using outbound automation to cover Tier 2+ accounts, you're leaving a massive amount of pipeline on the table.
 
At its core, our early playbook was simple.
 
Build content that earns trust at scale.
Then use automation to do the prospecting work of 19 reps.
 
The future of growth isn't bigger teams, it's systems that scale the output of small ones with good ideas.

content:
I've talked to 5 companies in the past year that were exploring M&A in our space. Multiple were bigger than us at some point, but made the same fatal mistake: they stayed point solutions.
 
Each of these companies' value came from a specific workflow or signal they had access to. But that strategy's just not resonating with buyers anymore. Here's why:
 
(1) AI is more powerful with lots of data
 
The best AI products use massive amounts of data to deliver value. Point solutions struggle to accumulate meaningful amounts of data, and are reliant on 3rd party integrations. This results in a more buggy and disjointed workflow for the user.
 
(2) AI is transforming how software is built, and it creates a winner-take-all dynamic.
 
It's not a secret - the best product teams are using Cursor and Claude Code to ship product at 2-3x the pace. The best teams ship faster, raise bigger rounds faster, and ultimately break out in a market.
 
I think you can still build a point solution and make a solid business out of it.
 
But if you want to build something big, you'll ultimately have to extend and become a platform, and ship many products.

content:
2 months ago, Ramp shut down the Outbound Automation program I helped build (OATs). People think that validates their take on outbound being dead. But they're learning the wrong lesson.
 
Ramp believed in outbound before I joined the company in 2020. When we started the OATs program in early 2021, Ramp had 3 SDRs, and millions of accounts to target. Automation and humans worked successfully in parallel because there was so much ground that 3 humans couldn’t cover.
 
But over the next 5 years, Ramp scaled from 3 to hundreds of outbound sellers. The focus (as I understand it) naturally moved from how do we support sellers. But Ramp has never wavered on outbound.
 
The real lesson from the OATs shutdown is not to extrapolate learnings from a 0.01% company to your situation. Ramp is alone in its ability to successfully deploy engineering talent towards distribution problems like outbound.
 
The future of outbound is bright, but it will be forged by giving sellers the power of AI and automation at their finger tips. Not by replacing them.

content:
At 22, I thought my career would be a straight line up and to the right. I quit that job 2.5 years in. 10 years later: I'm the CEO of an 80-person AI company. Here's a year-by-year timeline of what that winding journey looked like:
 
→ 22: Graduated from college and started what I thought was the best job ever. It was a super prestigious banking job, and I felt great about myself.
 
→ 23: Had a reckoning. I was miserable, working around the clock on work I hated.
 
→ 24: Made peace with banking and decided to make the most of it. I also figured out I wanted to be a product person.
 
→ 25: Got a random opportunity to join the SoftBank Vision Fund. I learned an insane amount about software companies and fell in love with the business model.
 
→ 26: Built Fisheye Surf as a side project. This is how I learned to build a full-stack application from scratch and knew for certain that building product was what I wanted to do. I also started at Ramp later this year.
 
→ 27: Got plopped into growth at Ramp, fell in love with it, and found out I was really good at it. I then helped scale the company from around $300M to $8B in valuation.
 
→ 28: Took on multiple teams and a bunch of direct reports, and learned how to actually lead an org. I also decided I wanted to start Unify.
 
→ 29: Left Ramp and started Unify. We built out the initial team and got to work, but it was incredibly hard. I ended that year knowing we didn't have product-market fit and not knowing how find it.
 
→ 30: We found product-market fit, figured out marketing, momentum, and LinkedIn content, and scaled the team to around 25 people.
 
→ 31: My most challenging year yet. I had to learn how to become a leader of leaders and attract really strong senior talent. I also had to exit people for the first time, which was emotionally brutal. Despite the personal obstacles, it was a great year for the business.
 
→ 32: I'm feeling more grounded than ever. I take the work very seriously, but I don't let it affect my mindset like I used to.
--
Looking back, 3 big lessons stand out:
 
(1) After my first job, I stopped optimizing for money. Financial outcomes still mattered - but I realized money wasn't what I cared about most.
 
(2) A lot of my success came from work I did outside my traditional job. Building a product for surfers had 0 commercial value, but it taught me how to be a product person. The only reason I was credible at Ramp was that I'd done that work on my own time.
 
(3) You need to surround yourself with excellent people because if you follow them, you'll end up in a good spot. I first saw this at Ramp, and it's been confirmed many times since. Good things happen where there are good people.

content:
We just flew Unify's 78-person team down to Cabo for 3 days. I decided to scrap the usual startup offsite 'playbook.' This was the best decision we could have made.
 
When I think back on the first 10 years of my career, some of my favorite memories from that era come from Centerview summer offsites and Ramp holiday parties. Not during scripted talk-tracks and exercises - but side conversations and organic interactions with coworkers.
 
So at our own off-site, we wanted to leave space for team members to spend time with each other and build relationships on a personal level (and to take home memories that they'd talk to their friends about for years to come).
 
This is hard to do when everyone is heads down working or stuck in meetings. So instead of filling the schedule with presentations and structured sessions, we just gave everyone a ton of free time.
 
We trusted each teammate to fill the empty calendar as they saw fit.

content:
Campfire grew outbound pipeline 200% in 5 months without hiring a single new rep.
 
In that time, the team sequenced 8,000+ qualified leads, generated millions in qualified pipeline, and cut outbound execution time by 80% by unifying their fragmented stack.
 
Here's how they did it with Unify. 👇
 
***
 
When we first connected with their VP of Marketing, Katrina Queirolo, Campfire was hitting a classic growth wall.
 
Just 10 months post-founding, they'd 10x'd revenue and shaken up the fintech space. But they couldn't keep up the massive momentum without either:

(1) Significantly increasing headcount
(2) Upgrading their GTM tech stack
 
At the time, they were running HubSpot for CRM, Apollo for prospecting, and Instantly for email automation. None of the tools talked to each other, and their Founding GTM Lead, Ryan Young, was spending hours manually warming and configuring mailboxes.
 
Katrina and Ryan talked it over and realized they could collapse all 3 into one system and move fast enough to keep up with intent with Unify.
 
Our Product Growth Strategist, Micaela, got them set up with automated Plays that connected all those pieces - intent signals, enrichment, personalization, and sequencing - while handling mailbox health in the background.
 
Within 5 months, Campfire sequenced 8k+ prospects, generated millions in qualified pipeline, and 5x'd their outbound program's speed, all while keeping headcount lean.
 
You may have needed 3 separate tools + more headcount in the past, but in 2026, a unified approach can help you break through the growth ceiling.
 
As Katrina said, "Unify enables us to capitalize on even the most subtle intent signals to transform interest into booked meetings. The platform has boosted our growth opportunities tenfold."
 
Huge congrats to Katrina, Ryan, and the entire Campfire team.
 
P.S. If you want to learn more, I'll drop a link in the comments to book time with our team 👇

I expect we'll see GTM engineers making $300-500k in 2026.
 
Next year, companies are going back to business fundamentals, which means compensating roles that actually drive revenue.
 
And whether you want to call them GTM engineers or growth engineers, these are the people driving pipeline at scale. And for the first time, they're going to get comped like closers.
 
When you look at the economics, it's obvious who should be getting paid.
 
AEs make $300-500k because they close deals and take a percentage of the revenue they bring in. The ROI on great closers is undeniable.
 
And doubling the pipeline coming into your business has a much bigger impact than improving your close rate.
 
The person who generates that pipeline deserves to get paid accordingly. They're driving the revenue - just earlier in the funnel.
 
I think 2026 will be the year a lot of people are going to wake up to this and start comping top-of-funnel on closed-won revenue because of it.

In 2025, we generated over $52M in qualified pipeline by switching our focus from quantity to quality and experimenting with our growth channels. Here's the full breakdown of our pipeline by channel:
 
→ Inbound remained our biggest channel
 
Inbound was by far the biggest driver of new revenue for us in 2025. It drove growth all year, including $541k of new ARR in October alone.
 
→ Outbound was the big breakout story
 
We massively scaled outbound this year, especially in the past 6 months. We did this by systematically building up our NBR team and leaning into it hard.
 
This has been a strong new revenue producer for us, and there's honestly still a lot more juice to squeeze. That's really exciting, as it gives us a lot of control over our own destiny.
 
→ AOB had its ups and downs
 
With some volatility throughout the year, our Automated Outbound Program drove between $150-200k of new ARR every month this year. While the last 2 months have been softer as we've refocused on quality, we're seeing early signs of success from that shift.
 
→ Performance marketing was our least efficient channel
 
Although we closed some revenue from it, it was definitely our weakest performer.
 
In the early days, this can be especially challenging to dial in because your product has to be super refined and your economics very well understood.
 
That said, having somewhere you can put dollars and get revenue out is valuable, especially in crunch times.
 
--
 
One lesson I'd share: When you have something that works, be very careful with it.
 
Earlier this year, we turned off performance marketing, thinking it'd be easy to turn back on. Turns out it's not as easy as flipping a switch.
 
--
 
Can't wait to get after it in 2026 and scale on this quality foundation we spent all year building.

content:
Account Executives are still clearing $300-500K+ per year. But here's the honest reality of what it takes to hit that number in 2026.
 
Back in the 2020-2022 ZIRP era, AEs could make killer comp + hit 100-150% to goal living off of inbound and working <40 hours per week.
 
Those times are gone - and I'm not sure they're ever coming back.

content:
Your NBR team should be your hungriest, hardest-working function. Our NBRs at Unify consistently hit 125%+ to quota, and it has nothing to do with efficiency hacks.
 
Our NBR team is in the office five days a week, and they're often the last people in the office every night. It's an input → output role, and you need to have a hustle mindset to succeed in such a high-energy function.
 
And I think a lot of companies get caught up trying to get really cute about how they can make their people really efficient.
 
And efficiency is important, of course. But in the early days, you just want to throw a lot of energy at the wall, see what sticks, and then refine the machine from there.
 
Of course, if you're going to set this standard, you need to compensate appropriately.
 
At Unify, we started with a very flat comp system where we paid NBRs based on meetings booked.
But we pretty quickly found that we needed to tune that quite a bit to get top performance. For us, that meant incentivizing more for bigger deals.
 
That's why we moved to a point system, and later layered on incentives for closed-won revenue. Now, reps are incentivized to bring in good logos so that they can get a cut of the revenue when they close.
 
The truth is, too many companies try to perfect the machine before they've proven it works. Get the energy right first, get people actually performing, and then build the systems around what's working. Not the other way around.

content:
The idea of the "AI-powered 10-person startup doing $50M+ ARR" is ridiculous.
 
Craigslist pulled this off already; they hit $1B in revenue with ~10 people on the team. With software it's always been possible to do a lot with a few people. 
 
The goal of a startup is to capture a nascent but rapidly expanding market, and the best way to do that is to have as many highly capable people as you possibly can.
 
Unless you’re building a business with an incredible network effect (like Craigslist), if you want to build something really meaningful you’re going to need a team of more than 10.
 
You can't vibe code a great product with 2 or 3 engineers that will rival something built by a talented 100-person engineering team. Most products with any complexity at all still need large engineering teams. 
 
And if you're saying, "I want to be a 10-person company," you're inherently accepting a slower product velocity. With how fast everything moves now, that's a losing proposition. Your competition will lap you.
 
If you want to build something great in 2026, you need more than a skeleton crew to do it.

Marc Benioff pioneered the stunt marketing playbook in the early Salesforce days with campaigns like:

content:
We do 10-20 references before we hire anyone for a manager or leadership role at Unify. At 68 people, a very good or bad manager has a profound positive or negative impact on the company.
 
References are some of the strongest signals we have. Here's the exact system we follow:
 
I start reference checking in the early stages of conversations with the candidate. I'll tactfully text people they've worked with to get a quick pulse check on if there are any red flags that I'm not seeing.
 
Great candidates get "They're one of the top 2-3 people I've ever worked with; I'd kill to work with them again," while good ones get "Here are their strengths and weaknesses."
 
If there's no rave reviews at this stage, I often move on.
 
When we get later stage, I like to ask them to name 2-3 people they've worked closely with and predict what each would say about working with them. Then I get in touch with those people and see how self-aware the candidate is.
 
Leaders aren't one-dimensional, so I actively seek out 1-2 critical reviews to understand their specific weaknesses and how they handle tough situations. These also help me to understand how they've grown. It's a red flag if they haven't made any strides in what was a glaring weakness 5 years ago.
 
This system has helped us filter down to the best talent - curious what signals others rely on for making leadership hires?

content:
Usage-based pricing is hated by pretty much every revenue leader I meet. Here's what we learned experimenting (and failing) over the past 18 months at Unify:
 
Usage-based pricing in developer products has been around for decades. AWS has trained technical buyers to think this way for 19 years. But go-to-market teams have always operated in a pay per seat model.
 
The typical VP of Sales or CRO comes in with a fixed budget for each tool they need. They need to stay within that budget, they need predictability. Otherwise the CFO pushes back. They're used to buying Salesforce for $100/seat/mo, etc
 
We didn't deeply understand this at Unify until 3-4 months ago. Before then, we thought usage-based pricing would be our main expansion lever. But we hit so much friction trying to expand accounts this way.
 
We hit a breaking point: we set expansion targets for our account management team, and they felt impossibly hard to hit.
 
So we stepped back and looked at companies with strong net retention (e.g., Pylon). Studying them outside in, the answer was clear: they expand on a per-seat basis. Business buyers already think this way, so the expansion process has way less friction.
 
I think usage-based pricing is the right end-state for revenue software as well, but it's going to take a while for this to play out.

A lack of focus on the data.

content:
We raised Unify’s $6.6M Seed in 2023, followed by a $12M Series A in 2024 and $40M Series B in 2025. The decision that investors were underwriting at each stage was totally different. 
 
Here’s what investors (actually) cared about most at each stage of growth:
 
--
STAGE 1: Seed ($6.6M from OpenAI, Thrive, and Emergence)
Question investors were asking: Would Connor and I be great founders?
 
When we first raised back in February of 2023, we had no product and no customers. Investors spent most of their diligence talking to us, and doing a ton of reference checks with people we’d worked with over the past 5 years. One investor went as far back as talking to my boss from 2019 about my character.
 
The decision to invest was predicated on their conviction in Connor and me to execute the idea for Unify.
 
--
STAGE 2: Series A ($12M from Emergence and Thrive)
Question investors were asking: Can Unify scale predictably?
 
We raised our Series A with <$500k of ARR, so objectively it was early. Investors spent most of their time thinking about whether our go-to-market motion was repeatable. 
 
They wanted to see net new revenue cohorts that were growing consistently, and driven by channels like outbound and inbound to show that we could land customers outside of investor intros.
 
Was there a clear path to $10M of ARR based on the early signals on customer health and our acquisition model?
 
--
STAGE 3: Series B ($40M from Battery, Emergence, and Thrive)
Question investors were asking: Can we build a $100M ARR business?
 
Our Series B was the first round where metrics like retention, expansion, and unit economics became a meaningful part of the conversation.
 
Investors also wanted to deeply understand our product strategy, and how we’d thoughtfully navigate our competitive landscape to get to $100M of ARR.
 
Hope this helps if you’re in the process of fundraising at any of these stages. If you have any questions, let me know in the comments and I’ll try to answer as many as I can.

content:
Here's what 9/9/6 fans get wrong: being busy is a bug, not a feature. Investors don't care if you work 100 hours a week if you still fail. There's no participation trophies in startups.
 
I believe conflating busyness with success is a mistake. In my experience, the biggest winners are rarely the busiest. The biggest winners are able to find real time and space for deep, long-term thinking which can't happen if you're running from fire to fire.
 
To be clear, many on the Unify team work 996, but my goal is that we build systems that are reliable and sustainable enough that we grow like a weed without needing that.
 
I feel the most unproductive when I'm pushing 100 hours a week. I have too many priorities and am usually not doing any of them well. On the flip side, I've seen teams working 40 hours per week that ship win after win.
 
Some people can identify the highest-leverage work, execute on it, and put wins on the board - and some people can't.
 
So if you're leading a team and still measuring success by hours worked instead of wins delivered, you're making a big mistake.

In 1995, Steve Jobs was asked about A players vs B players in software.
 
His answer: the difference between someone excellent and someone good is 50 to 1.
 
What Steve said in the actual interview:
 
"In most fields, the difference between the best and average is 2x or 3x. The best taxi driver gets you across Manhattan in 15 minutes instead of 30. The best cook is maybe 3x better.
 
But in software, the difference between the best person and an average person is about 100 to 1. The gap between good and great is 25-50 to 1."
 
He argues that the best people in software are exponentially better than average, so keeping a high talent bar is his job. The most important role that he played as an IC was to keep the talent bar high, and get rid of the B players.

content:
After building Unify's Account Executive team from 4 to 14 over the last year, I've realized quota attainment alone is not a good enough metric for screening sales talent. Here are the 3 most important signals I look for to spot great sellers outside in:
 
(1) President's Club
 
P Club means you were one of the best reps at your company that year. Not just good-elite.
 
It signals someone is motivated to be at the top of the leaderboard relative to an entire sales org. That's what I want to see.
 
(2) Top 10% rep
 
Rankings show strong relative performance. Similar to P Club, but even more bullet proof.
 
When I see "Top 10% rep" or "Top 3 rep" on a profile, I know this person consistently outperformed their peers. That competitive drive separates great reps from everyone else.
 
P Club can sometimes be a participation trophy. This one never is.
 
(3) Top seller at a company with a bad product
 
Here's one most people miss.
 
I'd rather hire a top performer from the second-place company in a category than pretty much anyone else.
 
Why? At the best companies, often the product sells itself. But if you're crushing it at the company in 5th place, you know how to sell when nothing is in your favor. This is impossibly hard.
 
--
 
Yes, quota attainment is important. But it's a flawed metric on its own.
 
If there's enough inbound demand, you can be in the bottom 25% of a team and still hit quota. These 3 metrics will make sure you find great candidates.

content:
The 9/9/6 work schedule is hot right now for startups - here are my thoughts.

I strongly believe that hard work is necessary to build a generational company. But I disagree with a lot about 9/9/6 and what it implies.

I’ve worked 6+ days per week for the last 140 weeks of Unify. My thoughts on hard work:
(1) Founders should be working 6 days per week
(2) Your best people will probably be working over the weekends because “they care. It’s not obedience-it’s compulsion”, well put by Cristina Cordova
(3) It’s about consistency - working one weekend so that you can post about it on social isn’t 9/9/6, it's marketing
(4) We interview specifically for people who are excited to rollup their sleeves and do hard work, and have proven it with their actions. Typically they’re doing work-related things outside of work

What 9/9/6 gets wrong:
(1) Yes inputs matter, but outputs matter more than inputs. Startups are pay for performance, there are no participation trophies
(2) We’re often generous in what we consider "work". Work dinners are social time for me, not work. Being selective of where to spend time is one of the biggest strengths I have at Unify
(3) Sometimes hours are no substitute for experience. Core product architecture decisions should be made by an architect in a few hours. Not a junior SWE in 10 hours

Long hours have always mattered at startups, but maximizing output per hour is what the best companies are built on

Impact per hour of effort is how you sustain a competitive advantage over the long-run

content:
Maintaining velocity at 63 employees looks very different than it did at 20 employees.
 
Building a startup is like building a machine where each team is a gear. If the gears spin independently, you get less output and velocity is worse. 
 
Connecting teams with the right feedback loops is the key to velocity at Unify. 
 
Here are the 3 feedback loops I’m focused on:
 
(1) Customer Support → Engineering
 
Every support ticket should change something at the company. Maybe it's clearer copy. Maybe a feature needs to be rebuilt. Maybe support needs internal tools to work faster. 
 
The goal: it should get continuously easier to support each customer over time.
 
(2) Sales → Post-Sales
 
Having a clean handoff between sales and post sales is key to a positive customer experience.
 
We used to be terrible at this. We'd do all this work understanding a customer, then show up to the first call asking "What does your company do?"
 
Now we're building AI workflows to extract all relevant context and hand it off seamlessly. Post-sales calls now start with: "Here's what we heard - anything you’d add?"
 
(3) Growth → Post-Sales
 
Different channels have dramatically different customer quality. We've found paid marketing customers consistently have worse retention than outbound.
 
If you have a retention problem, your channel mix is one of the first places I’d look.
 
--
These 3 feedback loops make sure that we’re continuously improving the machine.

content:
We announced Unify's $40M Series B last month. Over the last 2.5 years, we've raised Seed, Series A, and B rounds. These were the most important questions investors asked at each stage:
 
(1) Seed: Is this a high quality founding team?
 
Seed rounds are founder bets. Do the founders have unique experiences and perspectives on the space? Can they actually ship high quality product?
 
My background at Ramp and Connor's at Scale teed us up well to raise. We'd seen these problems before. We weren't coming into a new space trying to figure it out - we had strong opinions about the world of go-to-market and AI.
 
(2) Series A: Is the go-to-market motion repeatable? Are there signs of PMF?
 
Series A rounds in AI are still founder bets to a degree, but investors want to see product and PMF de-risked. We raised at <$500K ARR, which was early.
 
But we'd proven:
- We had some early customers raving about the product
- Closing new customers was repeatable (5-10 new customers per month)
- Product velocity - we were putting out multiple new features per week
 
The GTM motion wasn't scaled, but it was repeatable.
 
(3) Series B: Can Unify be a billion-dollar+ company?
 
That's the bet investors take at Series B. The questions and diligence went 10x deeper.
It was less about Connor and me as founders, and there was way more focus on:
- Is the team world-class? Had we been able to hire strong leaders?
- How quickly were we growing? Is there a clear path to us getting to $100M+ of ARR?
- How strong is our retention? Are we starting to see expansion?
- How much customer love is there?
 
The Series B was much more a bet on Unify as a company than it was on Connor and I as founders.

content:
We raised Unify’s $40M Series B in just 21 days.
 
We were pre-empted and raised without a formal pitch deck - here’s how we did it:
 
The Company
- We were a 2 year old startup
- Our team was ~35 total, 60% business and GTM and 40% engineering, product and design
- We still had 95% of Series A cash in the bank
- We had a team of 9 Account Executives, and our GTM motion was highly repeatable
 
 
The Story
 
Our space has been red hot in 2024 and 2025. There’s strong demand from customers and many companies are growing quickly. Investors want to place bets. 
 
From January to March 2025, we had 4-5 investors say “hey we’d be really interested in leaning in. would you consider opening up a data room?”
 
Fundraising is a full-time job. We wanted to make sure that if we leaned in, the round would materialize quickly. If it didn’t, we’d hurt momentum and waste energy.
 
We didn’t need the money. But we were direct with investors about the amount and valuation we wanted to raise. And investors leaned in.
 
I met with Dharmesh and Jason from Battery Ventures and there was instant chemistry. They knew our space cold. We weren’t selling them our ideas, they already believed them and had strategic insights. They’d done a dozen customer calls before we met.
 
They told us they wanted to lean in, and we agreed.
 
Over the next 3 weeks we sent over a handful of diligence items (customer cube file, and a few supporting slides) and had 4-5 calls.
 
And after 3 weeks we had a signed term sheet to lead our Series B.
 
–
Reflections from the Series B
 
The Good
 
- Having Alexander Lucey on the team. Alex joined as COO in January and after signing the term sheet he ran the whole fundraise process. I was able to stay focused on my day to day while he got the Series B done. He’s a killer negotiator and got us to a great place - thanks for everything you do Alex!
 
- Expectation setting. We explicitly told investors what we wanted for dollars and valuation. This ensured that when we were having investor chats they were leaning into the deal we wanted as much as they were Unify and our product.
 
- We read the room. At our Series A, we jumped the gun and got pulled into a raise prematurely. This time when we leaned in we knew that the investors were serious. Battery had done so much pre-work that we went from first conversation to signed term sheet in just 3 weeks.
 
Learnings
 
- Timing / tariff market crash. We got unlucky with timing and ran the process while Trump was announcing tariffs left and right. My guess is that we saw a ~15% valuation discount because of the timing. Out of our control.
 
- Don’t get pre-empted, run a full process. The best way to get all of the terms that you want in a round is to run a full process. If you have a single term sheet, you don’t have real negotiating leverage. 
 
Hope these learnings are helpful for anyone fundraising 🙂

content:
In 2.5 years since incorporation, we've scaled Unify to 56 people. There's plenty I would do differently. But if I had to start over tomorrow, these are the 9 things I'd do again:
 
(1) Pick a lights out Co-Founder. Being a founder is so much harder than I imagined. Having a Co-Founder (Connor Heggie) who is all-in like I am makes the journey so rewarding. I'd personally never be a solo founder.
 
(2) Pick a social channel and work at it every day. The teams that understand viral content today have an unfair distribution advantage. As a founder, its so important to figure out how to nail one. For us that's Linkedin.
 
(3) Hire the insanely optimistic. Startups feel impossible until they work - you want a team that enjoys the challenges, not one that uses challenges as a reason to quit. Avoid the people who want to flock to proven ideas and brands, you're too early for them.
 
(4) Be 100% in person. Serendipity is important in startups, you'll come up with some of your best ideas while walking to get coffee or talking over dinner. Tapping someone on the shoulder is infinitely better than sending Slacks.
 
(5) Be extremely intentional about the tone you set. Your culture should be polarizing because the right people are not looking for a "regular" job. I'd set the tone from day 1 that this isn't a 9-5 job and that its going to be intense.
 
(6) Be open minded about unorthodox talent. When I first spoke to Rhea, we weren't hiring. So we did a 2-week work trial, and her ability to tackle tasks with little input shined. So we created a role. You don't have the cash to compete for traditional talent in traditional ways, so get creative.
 
(7) Hire 2 Account Executives early. Once you have signs of product market fit, its time to scale. Bring on 2 sellers of different archetypes so that you can find out what qualities work with your buyers. Hiring 2 instead of 1 will accelerate learnings.
 
(8) Bet on outbound early. I'd hire 2 SDRs who have 6+ months experience before hiring AEs. The best companies always nail outbound, and outbound will help you hone PMF in the early days.
 
(9) Don't be afraid to experiment and fail. You're going to try a lot of things that won't work. That's okay, cut your losses quickly and learn from them. Velocity is the name of the game.
 
Being a founder at Unify is the most rewarding job I've had - hope these learnings are helpful 🙌

content:
We killed vibe selling at our Nashville offsite and introduced 3 new sales frameworks instead.
 
I've been deep in the trenches with the Unify sales team lately, listening to 30+ sales calls a week, and saw that our reps were operating with no shared language around deal mechanics and quality. Hassan Irshad, who leads Revops for us, immediately called this out when he joined.
 
"This deal should close" isn't a sales methodology, and already isn't scaling at 12 AEs. So here are the 3 new frameworks we're using to drive sales execution:
 
(1) SPICED
 
This framework helps our team structure discovery and qualification, and ensures we don't miss key details.
 
- Situation - Understanding the prospect's current state and context
- Pain - Identifying the specific problems they're facing
- Impact - Quantifying how much those problems cost the business
- Critical Event - Understanding what's prompting the prospect to act now
- Decision - Mapping out their decision process and criteria
 
We're shooting for a win rate of 20-30% and SPICED is a critical framework in making that a reality.
 
(2) BANT: Budget, authority, need, timeline.
 
Simple but powerful for determining if an opportunity is qualified or not. For inbound leads, prospects need to satisfy 3 of 4 criteria. For outbound, we require 2 of 4 since timing is harder to control for. This framework keeps our pipeline clean and focused.
 
(3) Problem Aware vs. Problem Unaware
 
We bucket every prospect into 1 of 2 categories: problem unaware and problem aware.
 
Problem unaware prospects get 5-10 minutes of education upfront on the category. For problem aware prospects, we skip the education and go straight into deep discovery about their specific pains and use cases.
 
By segmenting our prospects, we stop treating every call the same way and start meeting them where they are in their buying journey.
 
--
 
We're still implementing these frameworks, but we're already seeing a +5% rise in win rates 📈

content:
To build a $1 billion+ company you need to have 5+ channels that each drive a meaningful portion of new revenue. Here’s our framework for standing up a new channel:
 
At Unify we have 4 channels that drive a meaningful portion of revenue (inbound, outbound, automated outbound, and paid marketing)
 
The levers that we pull to get the most out of each one:
 
(1) New experiments
(2) Iterating on initiatives that exist
(3) Unit economics
 
Channels mature over time. These are the phases we see as we’ve grown Unify to nearly $10M ARR. I’ll use our AOB build-out to show each of these in action. We took this channel from 0% to 15% of revenue over the past 18 months.
 
Phase 1 (Months 0 to 3) 
 
All of your focus should be on new experiments and creating multiple green shoots that can deliver recurring, quality pipeline for the business. As a rule of thumb, strive to have 3-5 experiments driving at least 4 demos per month.
 
Spend zero time on unit economics and only a little time iterating on what exists.
 
For us, this phase was when we started launching AOB with website intent and new hires-and started seeing early results for both.
 
Phase 2 (Months 4-12)
 
New experiments continue to be a big focus, but iterating on existing experiments now becomes a more meaningful lever. You should be looking at your CAC payback period and knowing that you’ll need to be below 24 months soon.
 
Here, we launched another 20 plays that incorporated many more signal sources.
 
Phase 3 (Months 12 and beyond):
 
You should be achieving a 12-24 month CAC payback period, channels need to make financial sense in phase 3. Continue to experiment to find new pockets of incremental pipeline.
 
We started monitoring our credit consumption in this phase to make sure we feel good about where we’re at. We’ve also gotten our CAC payback period well below 12 months.
 
Save this breakdown for future reference the next time you launch a new GTM channel.

content:
We completely changed our pipeline strategy at Unify and meetings booked decreased 34% Q/Q. But closed-won revenue is up by 58%. Here's what we learned from focusing on pipeline quantity over quality.
 
I’m a growth person by background, so my instinct is to always drive for more pipeline. Historically, we measured success by meetings booked (Stage 0 opportunities) instead of qualified opportunities (Stage 2). That had its time and place, but it became a mistake.
 
This obsession with quantity was killing our sales team's productivity. They were drowning in low-value meetings with non-ICP customers - we were closing less than 10% of deals when the our goal is 20-30%.
 
So we flipped our focus to quality and reoriented our strategy to solve this. Here's what changed:
 
(1) New North Star metric: S2 qualified pipeline, not S0 meetings booked
 
(2) Trimmed channels and doubled down on others: We cut programs that were driving unqualified meetings. Some of performance marketing and automated outbound were big culprits. We doubled down on outbound which has yielded the highest quality meetings for us.
 
(3) ICP discipline: Stopped booking meetings below our target company size
We’re already seeing the impact: win rates have risen from 8-10% to ~15%, and continue to climb.
 
In 2.5 years of building Unify, the consistent lesson for me is that the job is never finished: growth isn't linear, and sometimes you have to take one step back to take two forward.
 
Happy to dive deeper into any of this if helpful - drop questions below.

content:
Everyone's doubling down on enrichment in 2025. But they're betting on the wrong horse. The puck is moving toward agentic workflows, not cleaner CRM data.
 
Clay is amazing for enrichment, but most companies I talk to misunderstand where enrichment sits in the GTM landscape of the future.
 
When you use an enrichment provider, you're basically saying, "feeding data to reps through Salesforce is the best way to engage on it." We do this today, too. There's absolutely value in it.
 
But think about where the world is evolving to over the next 2-3 years. Instead of enriching leads and having a rep manually decide to email them, what if a future system identifies the signal, qualifies the prospect, writes the copy, and sends a personalized email automatically?
 
The next couple of years will be defined by transformative shifts like taking entire workflows that used to require humans and automating 100% of them via AI and data. It won't be defined by making Salesforce data cleaner.
 
Most companies I talk to are still asking, "How do I get better data to my reps?"
 
The right question is, "How do I eliminate the need for reps to make these low value decisions in the first place?"
 
Enrichment wasn't wrong. But it's the analog 1.0 of go-to-market. The puck is going toward a future state where the systems own end-to-end workflows. If you're investing heavily in enrichment, you're optimizing for yesterday's paradigm.
 
Keep your eye on the horizon - workflows are evolving quickly.

content:
This might get me into some fights with AI SDR companies, but I don't care. Billboards across SF are filled with AI SDR companies saying "Stop hiring humans" or "The era of AI SDR is here." I couldn't disagree with this take more.

The constant debate about AI is whether it's replacing humans or augmenting labor. But both of these schools of thought miss the point: you're selling to a human on the other side of the table.

That human will buy your product, and then another human at their company will have to deploy it and use it on a regular cadence. So even if AI takes away work that humans used to do, someone still needs to manage it, optimize it, and make decisions about it.

People are so stuck on the AI debate that they forget that all software replaces work that humans historically did. Humans just evolved the work that they did. And found better things to spend their time on.

This is why we're still hiring humans at Unify instead of replacing team members with AI. Because there will always be things AI can't replace, like:

(1) Cold calls: Using AI for this is illegal. Plus the best cold callers are 100x better than AI.
(2) Relationship building: AI can't read between the lines, build genuine rapport, or pick up on the subtle buying signals that humans naturally catch in conversations.
(3) Meet people in person: if I could replace all my zoom meetings with coffee chats I'd do it in a heart beat. People naturally agree more in person.

Yes, AI helps us scale outbound, but humans are what make the entire go-to-market engine actually work.

I don't care if this burns any bridges with AI SDR companies. Those billboards are selling a fantasy.

Today we're hyper-focused on how we segment our TAM at Unify. 3 months ago when we analyzed our closed-won data, we found that 50% of our reps time was wasted on bad fit accounts. So we're scoring the 330,000+ accounts in our Salesforce instance to identify the top ~50,000 to drive clarity and focus.
 
We're doing a massive enrichment exercise to build a proper account tiering structure for our sales and growth team. We used to operate with very little definition of ICP. That was fine up to ~3-5 reps, but as we've scaled our AE team beyond 10 reps that stopped working.
 
Reps were spinning their wheels on accounts that were never going to close. Defining pipeline quality was hard. New hires took longer to ramp because they had to figure out what our ICP was from scratch.
 
We realized we needed to get a lot more deliberate about who we're going after.
 
So we're building out our TAM with detailed account scoring and tiering based on data points that we've seen correlate with success.
 
A few of the many data points we're going to be tracking:
(1) How many SDRs and AEs the company has
(2) What CRM the company uses (from job posting data)
(3) Website traffic volume
(4) Customer count
(5) Does the company have a growth team
 
I'm bullish that this new way of account scoring is going to level up how we think about ICP

content:
This week the Unify NYC team is moving into to our 1st dedicated NYC office at 665 Broadway. I get asked often if being bicoastal between SF and NYC is worth it.
 
Honest answer: It's complicated, but the benefits have outweigh the challenges. Here's why we decided to do it and what it's meant for Unify.

Startups are all about talent, and we intentionally decided to bet on being bi-costal because we believed it would allow us to recruit the best talent.
 
In 2023 as a seed stage company, we did everything we could to get the best talent to join the team. Hyewon, our Design Lead, and Fabian, our Eng Lead, were in NYC and couldn't move. If we wanted our team to be SF only, we never could have hired them.
 
So we set up a shared office space that we've been consistently expanding as our team has grown in 2024 and 2025.
 
Having a New York presence has absolutely helped us to land talent across product and go-to-market. Today our NYC team is the same size as our SF one.
 
Having a sales presence on the east coast also matters, nothing beats selling in person.
 
But there's absolutely friction that comes from having 2 offices:
(1) Costs: 2 offices, travel back and forth, it all adds up. It's cheaper to have one HQ
(2) Culture: we've tried to be maniacal about trying to maintain our culture, and keeping the core values consistent across both offices. But doing so takes serious effort from the founders. This means that Connor and I are traveling often and spend a lot of time in our NYC office
 
If I could migrate everyone to a single office, I 100% would, but that's not realistic, and not the best thing for Unify.
 
We're stoked to be moving into 665 Broadway, with it we're entering a new chapter of the Unify story.

content:
In Q1 we improved our monthly gross retention by 5% by deeply focusing on ICP.
 
Here's what we learned:
 
For our first 12 months of selling, we closed any deal we could get, as most startups do. We were selling to 5-person startups and 1,000+ employee companies, and everyone in between. Growth was great, pipeline was strong.
 
But then churn started to pick up. 
 
We realized that for companies who don't have product-market-fit, we were struggling to get them to consistent meetings booked.
 
In Q1 of this year we had to take our medicine and tighten up our ICP. As a founder, that trade-off can be tough - it hurt to watch fewer deals come in. But it ultimately paid off:
 
(1) Our new customer ACV is up +101% since December
(2) Monthly gross retention has improved by 5% since February
(3) We've 4x'ed the number of $100k+ ARR customers we have
 
What I've learned is that investing behind ICP is something we need to be continuously doing. Even when we take a bet to go broader, be intentional about what this will do to your ICP and be aware of the risks.
 
By narrowing focus on ICP, we were able to dramatically improve customer health in just 3-6 months.

content:
Companies like Cursor and Together AI took less than 2 years to hit $100M of ARR, primarily driven by word-of-mouth. But surprisingly, I find the fastest-growing AI companies care deeply about outbound, too.

This generation of companies has a stronger sense of paranoia and a deep understanding that the era of "if you build it, they will come" is over. Today distribution trumps product. The products and companies that are winning are the ones who have a unique distribution advantage.

Even if you're running a top 10% company inbound isn't enough. Here's why the best AI companies care about outbound:

(1) You'll acquire higher-quality customers
Outbound lets you be opinionated about your ICP and consistently refine it. You don't just have to accept whoever shows up at your door. ACV, retention and expansion rates all tend to be better with outbound customers.

(2) You'll learn what resonates faster
To nail outbound, your messaging needs to be on point. You can quickly build intuition for which messages resonate with your ICP. This turns into a continuous feedback loop for iterating your pitch. It also helps you to understand where your customers see value in your product. It's rarely where you expect. 

(3) You control your own destiny:
If you're only inbound and your main channel gets interrupted (the algorithm changes, ad costs increase, or the channel goes down completely), your pipeline can dry up overnight. Outbound gives you a lever you have total control over. 

The fastest growing companies in 2025 aren't asking if they should run inbound OR outbound, they're talking to us about how they can run both.

Today is day 878 of Unify. If I could give myself one piece of advice on day 1, it'd be to invest in top-of-funnel (automated outbound, social) 6 months earlier than we did.
 
Coming out of 2023, the fundraising environment was rough. The fundraising market was in a hangover coming out of 2021 and 2022.
 
So we tried to be extremely efficient and lean as a company. We were conservative about every hire and every dollar we spent – which was fantastic for keeping burn low. But as a result, we underinvested in top-of-funnel ideas early on.
 
In retrospect I think this was a missed opportunity. Here's what I would have done differently:
(1) Start posting 5 days per week on Linkedin a year earlier than I did
(2) Hire 2 BDRs immediately after finishing our design partner program
(3) Start our automated outbound program with Unify at the same time
 
Automated outbound generated $7M in pipeline for us in 2024. And social content drove 19% of our inbound pipeline. This could be even higher had we started earlier.
 
In the early days, over-invest in top-of-funnel to maximize learnings.

content:
I'm sick of seeing AI SDR companies prey on startups. I've spoken to dozens of revenue leaders churning from AI SDR solutions that promised pipeline but delivered zero results.

Series A and B-stage companies are just getting started with outbound and AI SDR companies pitch an easy to use solution that just "works."

They promise the world: "Replace your SDR team, scale infinitely, book meetings while you sleep!" But here's what's actually happening behind the scenes:

Spray-and-pray outreach with light AI personalization.

These tools fail so consistently because AI SDR solutions are trying to replace human judgment rather than amplify it.

They pull lists of thousands of prospects and blast generic emails with random personalization (e.g. "I saw you went to Stanford!"), hoping something sticks.

But all this does is burn email deliverability and spam potential customers. Or even worse – it trains your market to ignore you.

Generating pipeline requires human creativity and strategic judgment that can't be fully automated. The best human SDRs reach out at the right time (e.g. when the buyer shows a relevant signal), craft messages that speak to specific pain points, and elegantly handle objections. 

I'm not saying that none of the SDR workflow can be automated. AI is insanely helpful for tasks like research, account qualification, intent signal detection, etc. (all of which we do at Unify).

But the truth is, most Series A and B-stage companies are best off figuring out outbound for the first time with a strong agency like SendtoWin or Outbound Gen. Or by hiring a top decile SDR to start the program. You need someone who is ready to experiment, test hypotheses and learn quickly from mistakes.

Once you're repeatably finding success with manual outbound, you're ready to scale.

content:
We use Attention to continuously learn from 500-1000 sales calls per month. My top focus is on making Unify an AI-first company. Attention is a huge piece of that, and helps us level up sales and product development.
 
Instead of tracking competitive intel by spending hours listening to every call recording and taking notes, anytime a prospect mentions our competitors on a call, our entire team can listen into how the rep handled the situation.
 
How this works:
(1) Attention records all sales calls
(2) AI extracts the exact context of what prospects said, this is based on a custom prompt
(3) A workflow in Attention sends an instant Slack alert to sales + product
(4) We include a snippet of the conversation so we can hear the context around the mention
 
Today it's possible for product and sales to know everything that's being mentioned on sales calls. In 2025 every business needs to be AI-first.

content:
If you're a Series B-D founder in 2025, the right growth leader will inflect your business. Here are the 4 things you should look for in a potential hire:

(1) Unorthodox backgrounds

You're not looking for traditional marketers. You want analytical problem-solvers who are first principles thinkers. You want someone who sees growth as a science to be tested and iterated on. You want to hire future founders.

Our Growth Lead Rhea had zero marketing background. Her background (Bridgewater Associates + Kalshi) was unorthodox. 

(2) Deep understanding of unit economics
 
Growth leaders are constantly making go/no-go decisions based on unit economics. Unit economics are a guiding force in startups. Great growth operators have strong business intuition for if a bet is worth taking based on the economics.

I prefer CAC payback period as my north star for unit economics. As a rule of thumb, <12 months is great, 12-24 months is okay, 24+ months and you need to improve.

Some operators I've seen who've mastered this:
Dennis Sevilla - COO & CFO at Guru
Max Beauroyre - Head of Growth at Abacum
Edouard U. - Growth Lead at Pigment

(3) Xfn skills
 
Growth sits at the intersection of sales, product, and engineering – teams with very different priorities. Great growth operators can work across these functions seamlessly to deliver impact. It's simple, but not easy to find in practice.

(4) Experimentation and data driven
 
Diving into pivot tables, SQL queries and dashboards should be second nature. The right candidates will want to validate every decision with data.

In my experience growth experiments fail 2 out of 3 times. The best operators double down on the winners to squeeze them for every ounce of output. And they see the shimmers of hope in the experiment that failed for the wrong reason.

A great growth leader is your next 10x hire. Go find them!

content:
In the last 4 weeks, I asked 28 growth and revenue leaders at hyperscaling Series B-F startups how they're winning their categories. Here are the 6 strategies they shared:

(1) Nailing ICP
 
A founder I spoke to recently 3x'd their win rates just by narrowing focus—it dramatically improved their sales process for ICP accounts.

Trying to sell to everyone too early stresses your product team. In March and April, we narrowed our ICP to deliver a 10x better experience to a focused market segment.
 
Be crystal clear about who you're building for today, who you'll build for tomorrow, and who you'll never build for.

(2) Dominating social

LinkedIn powered 19% of Unify's inbound pipeline last year. In the last 30 days alone, we generated 64 inbound demos from LinkedIn.

The compound effect is real—we routinely hit 250,000-500,000 impressions/week. But it took 6 months of consistent posting before the channel really took off.

(3) Leveraging warm investor intros

I met with a breakout startup recently that books enterprise pipeline primarily through investor referrals. The credibility earned from a trusted investor can open doors quickly that may take months via cold outreach. Use your network, especially if you're targeting the enterprise.

5 of our first 10 customers at Unify came from investor intros. We continue to win with this strategy as we add new investors to our cap table.

(4) AI-first operations

High-growth companies are rethinking how they build teams in an AI-first world.

At Unify, we use Pylon to automate 25% of support tickets for our growth customers. The goal is to increase % of tickets resolved with AI.

We also automate competitor research and call insights with Attention. We want to have continuous feedback loops from what our customers are saying on calls to our entire company so that no context is lost.

(5) 10x outbound sellers

Spray-and-pray is dead. Hyper-targeted outreach is thriving. The best BDR teams operate like outbound engines. They use real-time signals to craft 1:1 personalized outreach. Cold calling and LinkedIn are still effective channels, and you need humans for both.

(6) Sales development as a talent pipeline

Outbound is a hard job. The sellers who are successful in outbound are often great fits in other roles. I met a sales development leader at a public company who referred to her job as 50% delivering pipeline, 50% building a talent machine.

Our SDR-to-AE promotion track has been extremely successful. In 13 months, we've promoted 3 SDRs to AE. Tameem went from NBR to commercial to mid-market AE all in one year. Nikko and Sam Seiler have both recently moved from SDR to AE.

Outbound is great practice for closing. If you excel at that, you'll be successful as an AE.
--
Go-to-market is evolving insanely quickly, and the best teams are always looking for alpha with new plays and strategies.

Test some of these strategies out for yourself. Please drop anything I missed in the comments 👇

content:
If you sat in on Unify's board meetings, you'd think everything was broken. 

I used to dread board meetings. Now, they're the most valuable 90 minutes on my calendar. And the new way we run our board meetings has helped us grow ARR 9x Y/Y. 

We used to spend the 90 minutes running through slides full of data. And the more I think about it now, the more I realize we were wasting everyone's time.

A lot of founders believe board meetings are for the investors. To update them. Share numbers, etc. And yes, updates on metrics are part of it.

But a few months ago I got a great piece of advice from a mentor that "Board meetings are for you as founders. Use the time however is most valuable to you."

So we pivoted and now we use the full board meeting to spend 90 minutes on the biggest 2-3 problems we're facing. Since we've narrowed focus we can go much deeper on a few topics.

So, in our last board meeting at the end of 2024, we switched things up. All 40 slides were sent 2 days before the meeting so everyone could pre-read. During the meeting, we only covered about 5 slides.

For the full 90 minutes, we went deep on our biggest insecurities about the business. Out of that came multiple action items including a renewed focus on ICP (ideal customer profile). We made a clear strategic decision to build a deeper product experience for a narrow list of users. More to share on this soon 🙂

I’m thankful to have such a great group of thought partners in our board room. We wouldn’t be where we’re at right now without folks like Jake, Yazan, Vince, and Avery.

content:
Unify’s category of AI and go-to-market is insanely crowded. But as an operator building in the category, it feels like each company has a very different set of core beliefs. And these beliefs shape products and features we all build.

Here’s what we believe at Unify:

(1) Our north star metric is positive customer interactions

The goal of the products we build is to facilitate more positive interactions with your prospective and current customers. Every feature we ship is prioritized against this metric. When we drive this up, we know that we’re delivering more value for our customers. Both AI agents and humans can have positive interactions.

(2) AI agents are the future

We assume that 90%+ of the tasks sellers do manually today will be automated by data enrichment and AI seamlessly woven together. Today, nailing agentic experiences is quite difficult. While we’ve seen early successes, we’re far from the finish line. We’ll continue to iterate and push the realm of what’s possible here.

We’re not very interested in analog enrichment and sales engagement workflows of the 2010s because they are not the future. These are check-the-box features for us. We index most of our creative energy towards thinking about an agentic future.

(3) Sellers who do prospecting will work out of Unify every day

Pipeline generation will revolve around Unify. Humans are an incredibly important part of the system-of-action that we’re building. Human touch remains the differentiator in sales today and that will only be more true over the coming years. But there’s so much that we can do to make the marginal 5 minutes 100x more powerful for a human seller. We’re excited about building a product to make this a reality.

--

By staying focused on these beliefs, we're building technology that enables more positive customer interactions at scale – whether those interactions are with humans or AI agents.
